notes.meaning: When the fifth angel sounds his trumpet, John sees a star that had already fallen from heaven to the earth. This star represents a fallen angel, often understood as Satan or an evil prince, who is given the key to the abyss, the deep pit where evil spirits are confined. He has no authority on his own, for the key must be granted to him by God before he can open the pit. God remains in complete control even when allowing dark forces to act.

differ.view: Some older commentators historically identified this fallen star as an earthly religious deceiver, such as the pope, who claimed supreme authority over the church.

notes.meaning: The fallen star opens the bottomless pit, and a dense cloud of smoke pours out like the smoke from a giant furnace. The dark cloud rises so high and spreads so wide that it blots out the sun and fills the air with blackness. This picture reveals how the powers of darkness spread confusion and hide spiritual truth from the world.

Out of the thick smoke, a swarm of locusts descends upon the land. These are not normal insects, but a demonic host sent from the pit and given the power to inflict agonizing stings like scorpions. They remind readers that God can use terrifying plagues to confront human rebellion.

These creatures receive a strict command not to eat the grass, green plants, or trees, which is what natural locusts would devour. Instead, their torment is aimed solely at people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads. God marks and protects His own people so that the plague cannot harm them spiritually.

differ.view: Some dispensationalists hold that this seal refers strictly to the one hundred and forty-four thousand Jewish believers during the final tribulation period.
Many teach that this seal marks all of God's elect, His chosen people, preserving them from eternal ruin in times of spiritual trial.

notes.meaning: The locusts are not allowed to kill anyone, but only to torment them for five months. The pain they cause feels like the fierce burning of a scorpion's sting, which brings terrible misery without taking a person's life. God places an exact limit on both how long this trial lasts and how much harm the enemy can do.

People will suffer so severely during this time that they will eagerly look for death, but they will not find it. They will desperately wish to end their lives, yet death will run away from them. This shows that death offers no easy escape when God brings the guilt of human sin to light.

John sees that the locusts look like war horses equipped for battle, wearing what appear to be crowns of gold, and having faces like human beings. This warlike look shows an organized, aggressive force that acts with human-like cunning. They boast a appearance of victory, though their power is strictly borrowed.

These creatures have long hair like women and fierce teeth like lions. The flowing hair gives them an alluring, deceitful look, while their lion-like teeth reveal their savage desire to tear and devour. Evil often presents a seductive exterior to hide its cruel intentions.

The locusts have chest armor resembling iron breastplates, and the sound of their wings roars like many chariots and horses charging into battle. Their iron armor makes them seem impossible for humans to injure or repel, while their noise creates widespread panic. No earthly defense can resist spiritual judgments on its own.

They have scorpion tails equipped with stingers, which give them the power to torment people for five full months. Their real danger does not come from devouring crops, but from the poisonous suffering they leave behind. God carefully limits the time and reach of the harm they can inflict.

Unlike regular locusts that have no leader, these demonic forces follow a king who is the angel of the abyss. His name is Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek, both meaning Destroyer. This title shows that his entire mission is to wreck lives and draw people into ruin.

The vision pauses to announce that the first woe has ended, while two greater woes are still coming. This marks a clear boundary between the trumpet blasts. It reminds readers that God's plan of judgment will move forward until every word is fulfilled.

The sixth angel blows his trumpet, and John hears a voice coming from the four horns of the golden altar before God. In the temple, this golden altar was used for burning sweet-smelling incense, which represented the prayers of the saints. The command for judgment comes from this very place, showing that God is answering the cries of His oppressed people.

The voice commands the sixth angel to release the four angels who are bound at the great Euphrates river. Because these angels were chained, they are evil spirits kept under restraint until the exact moment God appointed. The Euphrates was long known as a boundary where great enemy armies gathered against God's people.

The four angels are set loose, having been prepared for that very hour, day, month, and year to kill a third of mankind. Unlike the locusts who could only torment, this plague brings real death on a massive scale. God sets the exact schedule and limits of judgment long beforehand.

John is told the size of the cavalry army, which reaches two hundred million horsemen. This huge number pictures an overwhelming, terrifying force far greater than any human military ever seen. It reveals the staggering scale of the destructive army God permits to march across the earth.

The riders wear armor colored fiery red, smoky blue, and sulfur yellow, while the horses have heads like lions that breathe out fire, smoke, and sulfur. This frightening vision shows an army dressed in the very colors of destruction. Their breath brings terrible devastation to everything in their path.

A third of the human race is wiped out by the three plagues of fire, smoke, and sulfur blasting from the mouths of the horses. This deadly judgment shows the dreadful consequences of long-standing defiance against God. Even when judgment is severe, God still shows restraint by sparing the remaining portion of mankind.

The deadly power of these horses lies both in their mouths and in their tails, which are like snakes with biting heads. This unusual picture means the army can strike and harm people from every side. When judgment falls, there is no easy way for human pride to defend itself.

The people who survived these awful plagues still refused to repent, meaning to turn away from their sins. Instead of seeking God, they kept worshipping demons and handmade idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood that cannot see, hear, or walk. Hardened hearts often cling foolishly to helpless gods even under painful discipline.

The survivors also refused to turn away from their murders, their sorceries, their sexual sins, and their thefts. Turning away from the true God always leads to deep moral decay in how people treat one another. God warns that stubborn rebellion will eventually face His righteous judgment if people refuse His mercy.

differ.view: Some interpreters see this failure to turn to God as proof that judgment alone cannot change the human heart, because only the saving grace of the Holy Spirit can produce true repentance.
